strengths: Introduces a novel and timely method, mechanistic forecasting, that connects MLP value-vector probing with population-level preference prediction, extending interpretability work from binary factual correctness to distributional social-science outcomes.

The empirical scope is impressive: seven models (base and instruction-tuned variants across Llama, Mistral, Gemma, Qwen), six national elections, multiple persona attributes, and prompt templates, yielding a large-scale systematic comparison.

The paper asks an important question—whether latent internal signals can complement or outperform surface-level next-token probabilities for human preference prediction—and reports systematic heterogeneity across models, countries, parties, and attributes.
Probes are validated with held-out F1 scores above 96%, and the sign-inversion validation is a reasonable causal sanity check for selected value vectors.
The proposed entropy-based gating criterion, if validated, would be practically useful for deciding when latent aggregation may help.
Limitations such as white-box access and first-order approximation are acknowledged, and the paper appropriately cautions that latent activations do not imply the model holds beliefs or preferences.
weaknesses: The central claim that latent activations provide more reliable preference information is not cleanly identified: the paper compares latent aggregation only to next-token probabilities, without baselines such as temperature-scaled/calibrated probabilities, simple smoothing, uniform distributions, or direct probe-based predictions. Latent scores may win simply because they are less peaked and therefore closer to smoother survey distributions.

The win-rate analysis (Δ_k > 0) lacks statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, effect sizes, or correction for multiple comparisons across models, countries, parties, and attributes, making it difficult to know whether reported improvements exceed noise.

The entropy-gating result appears post-hoc and circular: the regression is fit only on Δ_k > 0 cases, and the 0.85 entropy threshold is not validated on held-out data or independent elections. This undermines the practical recommendation.

Probe semantic validity is not sufficiently established. High F1 may reflect lexical party cues rather than encoded political preferences, and the top value-vector tokens shown in Table 3 are frequently gibberish or generic fragments, raising concerns that selected vectors may promote party names rather than represent issue positions.

There is potential temporal leakage/contamination: for recent elections (e.g., US 2024, UK 2024), several evaluated models may have post-election knowledge in their training data. The paper does not report or analyze model knowledge cutoffs, which could inflate forecasting accuracy.

The evaluation may leak survey information: personas are sampled to match survey marginals, and the same survey data are then used as the benchmark. No train/test split or held-out election validation is used to assess out-of-sample predictive performance.

Reproducibility is limited: the paper does not provide code, data, or sufficiently detailed hyperparameters/probe-training procedures; probe data are manually harmonized from voting-advice applications, and the exact construction of the 24 million configurations is not clearly documented.

Presentation has gaps: Figure 2 is referenced but missing from the manuscript, several equations and aggregation steps are under-specified, and the exact derivation of Ψ_k^prob and the normalization of latent activation scores are not fully described.

The broader ethical implications of election forecasting are under-discussed. The impact statement dismisses societal consequences, yet using LLMs to predict or simulate voting behavior in high-stakes democratic contexts warrants careful consideration of misuse, representativeness, and manipulation risks.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and potentially valuable problem: using mechanistic interpretability to extract latent preference signals from LLMs for social-science prediction, rather than relying only on surface-level outputs.

The empirical scope is ambitious, covering 7 model variants, 6 national election surveys, multiple persona attributes, and 10 prompt templates, which if properly executed would provide broad evidence.
The MLP value-vector decomposition is clearly presented in Section 4.1, building appropriately on prior interpretability work (Geva et al., 2022; Elhage et al., 2021).

The use of representative election surveys with census weighting is an appropriate benchmarking strategy, and the paper includes a limitations section that acknowledges white-box access and first-order approximation issues.
The probe results (F1 > 96% on held-out data) suggest that party-related information is linearly decodable from intermediate representations, which is a useful starting point.
The entropy-based gating idea, if validated, could be a practical diagnostic for deciding when latent aggregation may help over output probabilities.
weaknesses: The central claim that mechanistic forecasting improves preference prediction is not adequately supported. The evaluation reports mostly win-rates without effect sizes, confidence intervals, or significance tests, and Figure 7 shows many Δ_k values near zero or negative; the title and abstract overstate the evidence.

The evaluation target is inconsistent across the paper: Figure 3 refers to P(party | category), while Figures 4–5 and the text refer to P(category | party) / category shares conditional on party. Equations (15)–(16) do not clearly define whether Ψ_k is a distribution over parties or over attribute categories, making the comparison with survey data ambiguous.

The method for converting latent activation scores into normalized probability distributions is not specified. A_{p,j} in Eq. (14) can be negative and unbounded, and Eq. (15) averages these scores, but it is never explained how Ψ_k becomes a valid probability distribution for JS or Wasserstein distance computation.

The entropy gating analysis is post hoc and circular: the authors estimate a regression focusing only on Δ_k > 0, then evaluate mechanistic forecasting only on attributes with normalized entropy > 0.85, using the same data. There is no held-out validation of the entropy threshold and no comparison against the probability baseline on the full set of attributes.

Probe/value-vector validity is questionable. The top value-vector tokens in Table 3 are mostly uninterpretable fragments (e.g., “aI”, “GHyde”, “æaKaiL½”, “uated”), not coherent party concepts. The sign-inversion validation is only a necessary condition, uses the same selection data, and does not causally demonstrate that these vectors influence vote choice in persona prompts.

Critical methodological details are missing: how sequence-level activation m_{i,p,j}^l is computed from per-token MLP activations, probe training data size and negative sampling, train/test splits, layer-selection sensitivity, IQR threshold sensitivity, prompt template construction, and how party tokens are chosen for multi-token party names.

There is a likely temporal mismatch in probe data: Vote Compass 2025 data are used for Canada 2019, New Zealand 2020, and UK 2024 surveys, while party positions can change substantially over time. This undermines the validity of the probes for the historical elections being predicted.

The base vs. instruction-tuned comparison confounds alignment with basic prompt-following ability. Base models may not produce meaningful next-token party probabilities, which can artificially weaken the probability baseline and inflate latent “wins” without isolating an alignment effect.

No comparison is made to a simple probe-based classifier applied to persona prompts, or to other internal readouts such as logit lens or linear probing. Thus it is unclear whether value-vector aggregation adds anything beyond standard probing.

The paper reports results over “24 million configurations,” but the effective evaluation is aggregated at the attribute level across a small number of attributes, parties, and countries. There is no correction for multiple comparisons, and win-rates can be driven by noise.

Reproducibility is limited: no code, data, or detailed hyperparameters are released. The probe data are manually compiled from voting advice applications and not made public, preventing independent verification.

The impact statement dismisses ethical concerns (“none which we feel must be specifically highlighted here”) despite election forecasting being a high-stakes application with clear risks of manipulation, misinformation, and representational harms.
Figure 2 is referenced but not included in the provided manuscript, and Table 3 tokens appear corrupted, further hindering evaluation of the claimed mechanistic evidence.

strengths: Introduces a novel and timely idea: using mechanistic interpretability (MLP value vectors) to extract latent preference signals from LLMs, rather than relying only on output probabilities.
Large-scale empirical study spanning 7 models, 6 countries, many persona attributes and prompt templates, providing a broad descriptive picture.
Methodological pipeline is clearly described, with equations for MLP decomposition, probe training, activation aggregation, and distributional comparison.
Highlights important systematic patterns (e.g., demographic attributes, high-entropy settings) and proposes an entropy-based gating criterion, which if validated could be practically useful.
Discusses limitations such as white-box access and first-order approximation, and appropriately cautions that latent activations do not imply LLMs 'hold' preferences.
weaknesses: The central comparison is confounded: the latent method uses external party-position data from voting advice applications to train probes and identify value vectors, while the probability-based baseline does not use this supervision. Any improvement may come from the extra party information rather than from latent representations per se.

No contamination control: several elections (e.g., US 2024, UK 2024) may be within or near the training cutoffs of the evaluated models, so the models could have memorized outcomes. The paper does not test on elections prior to model cutoffs or otherwise rule out leakage.

The entropy gating criterion is post-hoc and circular: the regression and threshold (entropy > 0.85) are selected on the same data used to evaluate Δ_k > 0, without held-out validation. This inflates apparent gains and limits practical guidance.

Lack of statistical rigor: win rates and median differences are reported without confidence intervals, significance tests, or correction for multiple comparisons across models, countries, parties, and attributes. Many results may be within noise.

The evaluation metric is not fully specified and may be inconsistent: the text alternates between P(party | category) and P(category | party); it is unclear how next-token probabilities are aggregated to party-level distributions, especially for multi-token party names or multi-party systems.

Probe validity is questionable: probes are trained on party statements from voting advice applications, which may contain explicit party cues; >96% F1 may reflect surface features rather than latent party concepts. Top value-vector tokens in Table 3 are often gibberish, undermining the mechanistic interpretation.

Persona sampling matches only marginal survey distributions, not the joint distribution of attributes and vote choice. This can bias conditional distribution comparisons in ways that affect both methods but are not analyzed.

No comparison to simpler baselines (e.g., linear probes on hidden states, multinomial regression on demographics, or probability-based methods that also use party descriptions). It is therefore unclear whether MLP value vectors add value beyond existing approaches.

Reproducibility is limited: code/data availability is not stated, manually compiled party-position data may not be shareable, and key details (party tokens, normalization, entropy definition, number of selected vectors, hyperparameters) are missing.
Figure 3's green points use oracle selection (choosing the better method per point), which is not a valid evaluation of a deployable method and overstates potential gains.
The impact statement is perfunctory and does not discuss potential risks of using LLMs for political preference prediction (e.g., manipulation, bias amplification, erosion of survey methodology).

strengths: Novel and timely framing: reframes LLM-based preference prediction as aggregation of latent representations rather than surface output probabilities, connecting mechanistic interpretability with social-science forecasting.

Large-scale empirical effort: 7 open-weight models, 6 national election contexts, 10 prompt variants, and 280k persona combinations; the appendix includes useful controls, layer ablations, intervention checks, and an ICL baseline.

The methodological pipeline is built on established interpretability ideas (MLP value-vector decomposition, linear probing, IQR-based selection, sign-inversion validation) and is described in reasonable technical detail.
Probe validation is relatively thorough: label-shuffled and random-weight controls perform near chance, and the paper reports strong held-out probe F1 scores.

Honest limitations and ethics discussion: the authors acknowledge white-box requirements, first-order approximation issues, binary probe limitations, and risks of misuse such as micro-targeting; an impact statement is included.
weaknesses: The central evaluation is under-specified and difficult to reproduce: it is unclear how latent activations (which can be negative) are normalized into probability distributions, how next-token probabilities are converted into comparable distributions, how multi-token party names are handled, and whether the compared quantities are P(category|party) or P(party|category). This ambiguity directly affects the main latent-vs-probability comparison.

The entropy-gating analysis is circular/selection-biased: the regression focuses on cases with Δ_k > 0, then relates entropy to those selected wins and evaluates high-entropy attributes. Improvements are therefore guaranteed by construction. The 0.85 threshold appears post hoc and is not validated out-of-sample, so it cannot support the claimed practical gating criterion.

Main results are modest and not statistically robust: win-rates are often not clearly above 50%, no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for win-rates, multiple comparisons across models/countries/parties/attributes are not corrected, and there is no aggregate vote-share accuracy metric. The abstract overclaims relative to the evidence.

Construct validity of the latent preference signals is not established: selected value vectors are validated mainly as directions that promote party tokens, and the non-political intervention is essentially expected by construction. There is no individual-level validation or comparison to standard political-science baselines showing that persona-induced activations encode vote choice rather than generic political sentiment.

Potential optimistic bias from data reuse: personas are sampled and weighted to match the same representative surveys used for evaluation, with no held-out election or survey. This may inflate latent win-rates and limit generalizability.

Reproducibility gaps: the code repository link is missing, probe training hyperparameters (optimizer, learning rate, batch size, epochs, party-token definitions) are incomplete, and manual data harmonization/normalization choices are not fully documented.

Presentation issues: notation is inconsistent (e.g., W_n vs. W_o, Ψ_k as a party vector vs. a distribution over categories), there are typos in tables, and the mapping from attribute-level distributions to party-level estimation errors in Figure 3 is unclear.

strengths: The paper tackles a timely and potentially important question: whether LLM internal representations contain preference-relevant signal that is not captured by next-token probabilities, and whether this can improve social-science prediction.

The empirical scope is ambitious: seven open-weight models, six national election contexts, multiple persona attributes, and ten prompt variants. The combination of probing, MLP value-vector decomposition, and aggregation is clearly motivated by prior mechanistic-interpretability work.

The authors include several useful validation checks, including probe controls (label-shuffled, random-weight, regression baselines), a layer-window ablation, sign-inversion-based vector selection, a non-political intervention, and an in-context-learning baseline.

The limitations section and impact statement are honest about white-box access requirements, the local first-order approximation, the complementarity of surveys and LLMs, and potential misuse for profiling or micro-targeting.
The entropy-gating idea, if properly validated, could be practically useful for deciding when to rely on latent versus surface-level estimators.
weaknesses: The central methodological construct is not convincingly defined: latent activation scores are not probabilities, may be negative when diametric vectors are included, and are normalized in an unspecified way before being compared to survey distributions. There is no calibration or probabilistic model linking value-vector activations to vote shares, so the distributional comparison is difficult to justify.

The evaluation target is inconsistent across the paper. Section 4.3 defines distributions over attribute categories, Section 4.4 refers to distributions for each attribute and party, Figure 3 describes P(party | category), and Figure 4 describes category shares conditional on party. This ambiguity makes the results hard to interpret and impossible to reproduce faithfully.

The probe validity is questionable. Probe F1 scores above 96% on held-out data are suspiciously high for identifying a party from voting-advice statements, answers, and comments, where lexical and issue-stance cues may trivially reveal the party. The controls do not rule out that the probes encode issue content or party-specific writing style rather than stable party representations.

The selected value vectors are not shown to mediate the persona-to-vote mapping. The non-political intervention demonstrates that scaling selected vectors can raise party-token logits, but it does not establish that persona-induced activations of these vectors causally drive vote-preference predictions or correspond to human preference distributions.

The entropy-gating analysis is statistically problematic. The authors regress distance differences focusing on cases with positive differences, then evaluate the entropy-gated subset on the same data. This is selection on the outcome and lacks held-out validation, so the proposed gating criterion is not supported.

Main win-rate comparisons lack statistical inference. There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, multiple-comparison corrections, or effect-size summaries for the central Δ_k comparisons. Several reported win-rates are below 50%, so the claim that mechanistic forecasting improves predictions is selective and overstated in the abstract.

The evaluation baseline is narrow. The main comparison is against next-token probabilities from persona prompts, while the in-context-learning baseline and other potential baselines are relegated to the appendix. There is no comparison to simple demographic, party-identification, or polling baselines, making the practical significance unclear.

Potential temporal and knowledge leakage is not addressed. The elections span 2019–2024, and the models have different training cutoffs; party-position data may also be post-election. It is not analyzed whether models had already memorized outcomes or candidate/party associations, which could inflate apparent preference prediction.

Reproducibility is weak. The code repository link is missing from the PDF, and key details are absent: normalization procedure, party-token extraction, Monte Carlo sample sizes, survey weighting, probe training details, layer aggregation, and handling of diametric vectors. Table 4's top-token examples are largely garbled or uninterpretable.

The claimed scale of 'over 24 million configurations' is not clearly justified or analytically meaningful. A large grid of persona-prompt-model combinations does not itself establish systematic coverage, statistical power, or mechanistic insight.

The mechanistic claims are overstated relative to the evidence. The paper does not demonstrate that the selected probes or value vectors are necessary or sufficient for party preference, nor does it show that latent representations contain exploitable information about human preferences beyond artifacts of probing, normalization, and post-hoc attribute selection.

Presentation issues compound the technical problems: typos and notation errors (e.g., W_n in Eq. 6, a brace mismatch in Eq. 8, 'TAXENS' in Table 4), contradictory captions, and small or unreadable appendix figures/tables make the paper harder to assess and reproduce.

strengths: Introduces a novel and well-motivated method: mechanistic forecasting, which identifies party-aligned MLP value vectors via linear probes, measures persona-induced activations, and aggregates them into distributional preference estimates that can be compared with survey data.
Large-scale empirical study spanning seven model families, six national elections, multiple persona attributes, and prompt variations, with a reported search space of over 24 million configurations.

Includes substantial validation: high probe F1 scores, label-shuffled and random-weight controls, regression baselines, layer-window ablation, sign-inversion necessity tests, non-political intervention experiments, and an in-context-learning baseline using the same party-position data.

Provides systematic empirical findings: latent activations help most for demographic attributes and in high-entropy settings, while gains for opinion-based attributes vary by country. The entropy-based diagnostic is a useful practical direction.

Reproducibility and responsible research practices are relatively strong: prompts, probe data, and code are released, and the impact statement clearly distinguishes latent statistical associations from LLM-held preferences while discussing misuse risks.
weaknesses: The central win-rate comparison lacks uncertainty quantification and formal statistical testing. No confidence intervals, paired tests, or multiple-comparison corrections are reported for the many attribute-party-model-country comparisons, so the main claims about improved prediction are not fully statistically grounded.

The entropy-gating criterion is derived from a regression on cases with positive distance differences and then evaluated on the same data with an arbitrary threshold (>0.85). This selection on the outcome makes the gate's practical usefulness difficult to assess without held-out validation or a pre-registered threshold.

Several methodological equations are imprecise or contain minor errors. For example, Equation 6 introduces both W_n and W_o without clarity, Equation 8 has brace mismatches, and Equations 15–16 do not cleanly specify whether Psi_k is a distribution over attribute categories or a party-activation vector, nor how distances are aggregated across parties and attributes.

The probability-based baseline is not described in enough detail to judge fairness. It is unclear how next-token probabilities are extracted for multi-token party names, how prompt variants are aggregated, and how competing party probabilities are normalized before comparing to survey distributions.

Probe-training details such as the number of examples per party, class balance, and exact training hyperparameters are largely relegated to the appendix or omitted, which limits immediate assessment of probe reliability and reproducibility.

The method requires white-box access and is evaluated on six Western democracies, so external validity and practical applicability are limited. The paper acknowledges these constraints, but they still restrict the reach of the contribution.
